story.head: Tired legs for the Mammoth
paras: The Mammoth are winless in three (0-2-1), while the Blues (8-8-2) beat Detroit 3-2 on Tuesday. This is a Central Division matchup, with the Blues seventh (tied for 21st in the NHL) and the Mammoth fifth (tied for 15th).

The Blues have played better than their record (.500) says: their chances are worth about .560, and their finishing has held them back. So have the Mammoth (.553 on chances worth .699), where their goaltending has held them back.

The Blues keep things calm after the whistle (lowest) and ice the puck less than almost anyone (2nd), but have struggled on the power play (31st). The Mammoth roll their lines more evenly than anyone (1st), rarely get pinned in their own end (1st) and let the point shots come and guard the net (1st). Utah has allowed 3.58 goals a game, the fourth most in the league. The Blues’ good looks will be harder to come by against the Mammoth.

Jimmy Snuggerud (10 G / 4 A / 14 P in 18 GP) is tied for the Blues’ scoring lead. Robert Thomas (3 G / 11 A / 14 P in 18 GP) shares it, with a point in six straight games against Utah. For the Mammoth, Clayton Keller (5 G / 20 A / 25 P in 19 GP) leads the way in scoring, with nine points in his last five games. Nick Schmaltz (9 G / 11 A / 20 P in 19 GP) has a team-high nine goals.

Joel Hofer (7-5-1 / .920 SV% in 13 GS) has been outstanding for St. Louis and is expected to start. Karel Vejmelka (6-6-0 / .867 SV% in 12 GS) has struggled for Utah so far, but is expected to start. Vejmelka has a .861 save percentage in seven starts against the Blues, well under his usual .897. Don’t read much into it: a goalie’s record against one team rarely holds up.

items.text: The Mammoth are newly without Nate Schmidt and Dylan Guenther, and have been without John Marino since Oct 17. Taking into account how much value each of these missing players usually adds, no team is missing more right now.
Jimmy Snuggerud has nine goals on chances worth about 4.3 goals, well above what his finishing usually turns chances into. Runs like that tend to cool off.
Nick Schmaltz is a game-time decision, NHL.com says.
